# Overview

This lab is practice with Seurat itself. Later labs will rely on you knowing
how to manipulate and interact with the Seurat object.

**Dataset.** `ifnb` from the SeuratData package: human peripheral blood
mononuclear cells (PBMCs), half left untreated and half stimulated with
interferon-beta (IFN-β). The object comes with cell-type labels already
assigned.

Here we load Seurat, and set a random seed.
```{r libraries}
library(Seurat)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(devtools)
set.seed(42)
```

# Part 0: Research the background biology (15-20 minutes)

Before you get started, do a little bit of research on what to expect:

1. Which cell types are found in PBMCs and in what rough proportions?

2. What does interferon-beta do to immune cells? Find 3-4 genes that are
expected to respond to this stimulus. 


Find a few papers that support your answers to the above.


# Part 1: Load the data and explore the object

```{r load}
devtools::install_github('satijalab/seurat-data')   # run once
InstallData("ifnb")                                  # run once
data("ifnb")
```

`UpdateSeuratObject()` converts the stored object to the version of Seurat
installed for this course. Run it even if loading appears to work.

```{r update-object}
ifnb <- UpdateSeuratObject(ifnb)
```

Convert the RNA assay to the current (v5) format, so layers behave the way they
will in later labs.

```{r convert-assay}
ifnb[["RNA"]] <- as(ifnb[["RNA"]], Class = "Assay5")
```

This will be the object you will most likely be working with when performing
single cell RNAseq data. If you work in a different ecosystem (python), you will
see different solutions (`annData`) that all attempt to solve the same goal of 
holding annotation information, counts, and all other analyses from the scRNAseq
workflow in a single object. 

Printing the object gives a short summary:

```{r print-object}
ifnb
```

A Seurat object holds several kinds of information about the same cells. These
functions let you look at each one:

| Function | What it returns |
| --- | --- |
| `ncol()`, `nrow()` | Number of cells (columns) and genes (rows) |
| `Cells()`, `Features()` | Cell barcodes and gene names |
| `Assays()` | The assays stored, for example `RNA` |
| `Layers()` | The layers in the active assay: `counts` (raw), `data` (normalized), `scale.data` (scaled) |
| `ifnb@meta.data` | The metadata: a data frame with one row per cell |
| `Reductions()` | Stored dimensional reductions, such as PCA or UMAP |
| `Idents()` | Each cell's current identity, used by many plotting and subsetting functions |

How many cells and genes are in the object?

```{r n-cells-genes}
ncol(ifnb)
nrow(ifnb)
```

A few cell barcodes and gene names:

```{r cells-features}
head(Cells(ifnb))
head(Features(ifnb))
```

Which assays does it contain?

```{r assays}
Assays(ifnb)
```

Which layers does the RNA assay contain?

```{r layers}
Layers(ifnb)
```

What columns are in the metadata right now?

```{r metadata-columns}
colnames(ifnb@meta.data)
```

Are any reductions (PCA, UMAP) already stored?

```{r reductions}
Reductions(ifnb)
```

What are the cells' identities right now?

```{r idents}
head(Idents(ifnb))
```

# Part 2: Work with metadata

The metadata is a data frame with one row per cell. Anything you can compute
about a cell can be stored there and used to subset, group, or color plots.

## 2a. Inspect it

```{r metadata-head}
head(ifnb@meta.data)
```

There are three ways to pull a metadata column.

```{r access-dollar}
# A character vector
ifnb$stim
```

```{r access-brackets}
# a dataframe
ifnb[["stim"]]
```

```{r access-slot}
# a character vector
ifnb@meta.data$stim
```

Use $ for everyday work, like reading a column (ifnb$stim) or adding one 
(ifnb$group <- ...). It returns a plain vector that works with table(), mean(),
and comparisons. Use [[ ]] when the column name is stored in a variable 
(ifnb[[cluster_col]]) or when you want several columns at once. It returns a 
data frame with cell barcodes as row names, so add drop = TRUE if you need a 
vector.

The `table` counts or tabulates categorical data.

Cells per condition by accessing the `stim` column:

```{r table-stim}
table(ifnb$stim)
```

Cells per cell type accessing the `seurat_annotations` column:

```{r table-celltype}
table(ifnb$seurat_annotations)
```

Cell type by condition, table can be passed two variables on which to group and
count by:

```{r table-celltype-stim}
table(ifnb$seurat_annotations, ifnb$stim)
```


The number and names of cell clusters is the unique number of `seurat_annotations`

```{r}
# Names of clusters
unique(ifnb$seurat_annotations)
```

The total number of cluster annotations
```{r}
length(unique(ifnb$seurat_annotations))
```

## 2b. Add columns

You add a column to the metadata the same way you add one to a data frame:
`ifnb$new_column <- values`, with one value per cell, in the same order as
`Cells(ifnb)`. 

Seurat also has helpers that compute per-cell values for you,
such as `PercentageFeatureSet()`, which gives the percentage of each cell's
counts that come from genes matching a pattern. Seurat built-in functions will be
the most common way of updating the metadata. 

**1. Percentage of counts from ribosomal genes.** What pattern matches
ribosomal gene names in human data? Check what it matched before using it.

"^RP[SL]" matches gene names that start with “RPS” or “RPL”, the two families
of ribosomal protein genes (small and large subunit). The ^ anchors the match
to the start of the name, RP matches those two letters literally, and [SL]
matches exactly one character, either S or L. Note that a few unrelated genes
will be caught by this pattern, which for now, we will ignore. 

```{r ribo-pattern}
ribo_pattern <- "^RP[SL]"
grep(ribo_pattern, rownames(ifnb), value = TRUE)
```

Call the PercentageFeatureSet function:
```{r percent-ribo}
ifnb[["percent.ribo"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(ifnb, pattern = ribo_pattern)
```


Inspect what the function added to the metadata
```{r metadata}
ifnb@meta.data
```


**2. Adding a new column** This will return `TRUE` for CD14 and CD16 monocytes, `FALSE` otherwise. 
This will create a new column in your metadata that is a manual cluster of two 
subtypes of monocytes that you've defined. You can manually add columns to this
metadata to help group your data in more flexible ways. 

```{r is-monocyte}
ifnb$is_monocyte <- ifnb$seurat_annotations %in% c("CD14 Mono", "CD16 Mono")
```

**3. Concatenating together multiple columns** Cell type and condition combined
into one label, for example `CD14 Mono_STIM`. You can also concatenate multiple
columns together to generate new labels or groupings. 

```{r group-column}
ifnb$group <- paste(ifnb$seurat_annotations, ifnb$stim, sep = "_")
```

You can see these two changes by accessing the `ifnb@meta.data`

## 2c. Subset and confirm

`subset()` keeps the cells that meet a condition written in terms of metadata
columns (or gene expression).

**Example 1: stimulated cells only.**

```{r subset-stim}
# The expression being evaluated is the stim column having the STIM value
stim_only <- subset(ifnb, subset = stim == "STIM")
ncol(stim_only)
```

**Example 2: CD14 monocytes from control cells only.** Conditions on two
columns are combined with `&`. The expected number is one cell of the cell type
by condition table.

```{r subset-cd14-ctrl}
cd14_ctrl <- subset(ifnb, subset = seurat_annotations == "CD14 Mono" & stim == "CTRL")
ncol(cd14_ctrl)
```

You can use the code block below to calculate some of these as needed:
```{r}


```

## 2d. Calculate these values

| # | Quantity | Your value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Total cells | |
| 2 | Total genes | |
| 3 | Control (`CTRL`) cells | |
| 4 | Distinct cell-type labels | |
| 5 | Genes matched by the ribosomal pattern | |
| 6 | Median `percent.ribo`, to 2 decimal places | |
| 7 | CD14 monocytes, both conditions | |
| 8 | All monocytes (using the `is_monocyte` column) | |
| 9 | T cells (`CD4 Naive T`, `CD4 Memory T`, `CD8 T`, `T activated`), subset by identity | |
| 10 | Cells with more than 1,000 genes detected | |
| 11 | Stimulated CD14 monocytes with more than 1,000 genes | |


## 2e. Split and merge

Later labs combine several samples into one object. Practice here by taking
ifnb apart and putting it back together.

**Split** into a control object and a stimulated object:

```{r split}
ctrl_obj <- subset(ifnb, subset = stim == "CTRL")
stim_obj <- subset(ifnb, subset = stim == "STIM")
ncol(ctrl_obj)
ncol(stim_obj)
```

**Merge** them back together. The merged object should have as many cells as
the original (row 1 of your table).

```{r merge}
merged <- merge(ctrl_obj, y = stim_obj)
ncol(merged)
```

Are the barcodes the same as the original, in any order?

```{r compare-barcodes}
setequal(Cells(merged), Cells(ifnb))
```

Compare the layers before and after merging:

```{r layers-original}
Layers(ifnb)
```

```{r layers-merged}
Layers(merged)
```

`merge()` keeps each object's data in its own layer: `counts.1` and `data.1`
come from the control object, `counts.2` and `data.2` from the stimulated one.
This is useful when you want to process or integrate samples separately. To
combine them into a single `counts` layer, use `JoinLayers()`:

```{r}
merged <- JoinLayers(merged)
Layers(merged)
```

# Part 3: The standard workflow

Set your choices here as you work through this part. Each value goes in the
decision log at the end of this part. Change these to what you choose to use.
You may use the default values. 

```{r choices}
n_variable_genes <- NA number of variable genes to keep
n_pcs            <- NA   # number of PCs to use downstream (set after 3c)
clust_resolution <- NA
```

## 3a. Quality control

```{r qc-violin}
VlnPlot(ifnb, features = c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.ribo"),
        group.by = "stim", pt.size = 0, ncol = 3)
```

```{r qc-scatter}
FeatureScatter(ifnb, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "nFeature_RNA",
               group.by = "stim")
```

This is normally where you would filter but this particular dataset has already
been filtered. We will look at filtering in a future lab with different data. 

## 3b. Normalize, find variable genes, and scale

**Normalize**

```{r normalize}
ifnb <- NormalizeData(ifnb)
Layers(ifnb)
```

**Find variable genes**

```{r variable-features}
ifnb <- FindVariableFeatures(ifnb, nfeatures = n_variable_genes)
head(VariableFeatures(ifnb), 10)
```


## 3c. PCA

Seurat requires the data to be scaled
```{r run-pca}
ifnb <- ScaleData(ifnb)
ifnb <- RunPCA(ifnb, npcs = 50, verbose = FALSE)
```

```{r elbow}
ElbowPlot(ifnb, ndims = 50)
```


## 3d. Neighbors, clusters, and UMAP

**Find neighbors**

```{r neighbors}
ifnb <- FindNeighbors(ifnb, dims = 1:n_pcs)
```

**Find clusters**

```{r clusters}
ifnb <- FindClusters(ifnb, resolution = clust_resolution)
```

**Run UMAP**

```{r umap}
ifnb <- RunUMAP(ifnb, dims = 1:n_pcs)
```

`FindClusters()` added one column per resolution. Which columns are new?

```{r new-columns}
colnames(ifnb@meta.data)
```

How many clusters resulting from FindClusters?

```{r n-clusters}

```


```{r plot-clusters}
DimPlot(ifnb, label = TRUE)
```


# Part 4: Use metadata with your results

## 4a. Color by metadata


```{r umap-stim}
DimPlot(ifnb, group.by = "stim")
```

```{r umap-split-stim, fig.width = 10}
DimPlot(ifnb, split.by = "stim", label = TRUE)
```


## 4b. Find markers and name your clusters

**Find markers for every cluster.**

```{r find-all-markers}
markers <- FindAllMarkers(ifnb,
                          min.pct = 0.25,
                          logfc.threshold = 0.5,
                          max.cells.per.ident = 500)
```

**Top 5 markers per cluster by fold change**

```{r top-markers}
top_markers <- markers |>
  group_by(cluster) |>
  slice_max(avg_log2FC, n = 5)
top_markers
```

**Canonical markers.** 

```{r canonical-markers}
canonical <- c("CD14", "FCGR3A", "MS4A1", "CD3E", "CD8A", "GNLY", "PPBP")
```

```{r dotplot, fig.width = 10}
DotPlot(ifnb, features = canonical) + RotatedAxis()
```

```{r featureplot, fig.width = 10}
FeaturePlot(ifnb, features = canonical[1:4])
```

```{r violin}
VlnPlot(ifnb, features=canonical[1:2])
```


**YOU DO NOT HAVE TO DO THIS**

If you were annotating your clusters by hand, you'd make plots like the ones
above and decide which marker genes indicate which cell types. You'd then
record those decisions in R as a named vector, made with `c()`. Each name is a
cluster ID, exactly as it appears in `levels(Idents(ifnb))`, and each value is
the cell-type label you've assigned to that cluster.

These are fake cluster names artificially generated just to illustrate how you'd
do it.

```{r new-names}
new_names <- c(
  "0"  = "new_label_0",
  "1"  = "new_label_1",
  "2"  = "new_label_2",
  "3"  = "new_label_3",
  "4"  = "new_label_4",
  "5"  = "new_label_5",
  "6"  = "new_label_6",
  "7"  = "new_label_7",
  "8"  = "new_label_8",
  "9"  = "new_label_9",
  "10" = "new_label_10",
  "11" = "new_label_11",
  "12" = "new_label_12",
  "13" = "new_label_13",
  "14" = "new_label_14",
  "15" = "new_label_15",
  "16" = "new_label_16",
  "17" = "new_label_17",
  "18" = "new_label_18",
  "19" = "new_label_19"
)
```


This would rename your idents to your new manual clusters
```{r rename-idents}
ifnb <- RenameIdents(ifnb, new_names)
ifnb$my_labels <- Idents(ifnb)
```

```{r umap-my-labels}
DimPlot(ifnb, label = TRUE, repel = TRUE) + NoLegend()
```

You can see that nearly every function we called updated the metadata with
it's calculation or result. 

```{r final-metadata}
colnames(ifnb@meta.data)
```

## 5. Using Clustree to determine cluster resolution

[Clustree](https://lazappi.github.io/clustree/articles/clustree.html#clustering-trees-for-scrna-seq-data)

Clustering resolution controls how many clusters you get: higher values split
cells into more, smaller clusters. There's no single correct value, and we can 
employ a very common bioinformatics strategy to perform a sweep over many possible
values and see which make sense. 

First, cluster at several resolutions. Try to choose values both below and above
the default resolution of 0.8. Each one adds a column to the metadata
(`RNA_snn_res.0.2`, `RNA_snn_res.0.4`, and so on).

```{r clusters-multi}

```

Then plot them as a clustering tree:

```{r clustree, fig.height = 8}
library(clustree)
clustree(ifnb, prefix = "RNA_snn_res.")
```

**How to read the tree**

- **Each row is one resolution,** lowest at the top.
- **Each circle is a cluster.** Its size shows how many cells it contains.
- **Arrows show where cells go** as resolution increases. A darker, more opaque
  arrow means a larger share of the lower cluster's cells came from that parent.
- **A cluster with one strong arrow coming in and one going out is stable:** it
  stays the same group of cells across resolutions.
- **A cluster that splits into two or more** is being divided. That split may be
  real biology, such as two subtypes, or it may be over-clustering.
- **Many faint arrows crossing between branches** mean cells are being shuffled
  between clusters. Clusters in that region are unstable, and a resolution there
  is probably too high.

**Questions**

- Which, if any, clusters stay stable across every resolution?

- At what resolution do clusters start splitting into many small pieces, or
  cells start moving between branches?
  
- How many cell types did you expect in Part 0? Which resolution gives roughly
  that number? Where it gives more, are the extra clusters real subtypes, a
  split by condition, or over-clustering?
  
- The dataset comes with cell-type labels (`seurat_annotations`). Use them to
  check your choice: at the resolution you're considering, does each cluster
  contain mostly one cell type, or are some cell types split across several
  clusters? A table of clusters against labels will show you, for example
  `table(ifnb$RNA_snn_res.0.8, ifnb$seurat_annotations)`.

- Remember we have cell labels which can aid you in this.

`FindClusters()` sets the cells' identities to the last resolution it ran
(1.2 here). Set them to the resolution you chose before moving on:

```{r set-resolution}
Idents(ifnb) <- "RNA_snn_res.0.8"   # replace with your chosen resolution
```

Color the tree by a marker gene's average expression to see at
which resolution a cell type first separates out:

```{r clustree-gene, fig.height = 8}
clustree(ifnb, prefix = "RNA_snn_res.", node_colour = "CD14", node_colour_aggr = "mean")
```

You can do this for other prominent marker genes to visualize cluster stability.

Try a few markers for different cell types, for example `CD14` (monocytes),
`MS4A1` (B cells), `CD3E` (T cells), and `GNLY` (NK cells). Do they all separate
at the same resolution?


You can also cluster by any numeric metadata column. Here we color by how many
cells are stimulated within a cluster. 
```{r clustree-stim, fig.height = 8}
ifnb$is_stim <- as.numeric(ifnb$stim == "STIM")
clustree(ifnb, prefix = "RNA_snn_res.", node_colour = "is_stim", node_colour_aggr = "mean") +
  ggplot2::labs(colour = "Fraction stimulated")
```

A cluster near 0 or 1 indicate that they are entirely comprised of control
or stimulated cells, respectively.
